content: Rifampin, also known as rifampicin, is a bactericidal antibiotic belonging to the rifamycin group. It works by inhibiting bacterial DNA-dependent RNA synthesis through the inhibition of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Rifampin is a semisynthetic compound derived from Amycolatopsis rifamycinica (formerly Amycolatopsis mediterranei or Streptomyces mediterranei). It is commonly abbreviated as R, RMP, RA, RF, or RIF in the United States. The discovery of rifampin traces back to 1957, when a soil sample from a pine forest in the French Riviera was analyzed at the Lepetit Pharmaceuticals research lab in Milan, Italy. A research team led by Prof. Piero Sensi and Dr. Maria Teresa Timbal identified a new bacterium producing a novel class of antibiotic molecules, which they named rifamycins after their fondness for the French crime novel Rififi. After two years of research, a more stable and effective semisynthetic molecule was developed in 1959 and named rifampicin. This compound, with a 4-methyl-1-piperazinaminyl group, is the most clinically effective form of rifamycin. Rifampin is also known by other names, such as rifaldazine, R/AMP, and rifampin in the U.S., and Rofact in Canada. Isoniazid, also referred to as isonicotinylhydrazine (INH), is an organic compound and a first-line medication for the prevention and treatment of tuberculosis. Although it was first synthesized in the early 20th century, its anti-tuberculosis activity was only reported in the early 1950s. Several pharmaceutical companies, including Roche, attempted to patent the drug simultaneously but were unsuccessful. Roche launched its version, Rimifon, in 1952. Isoniazid was initially tested in Many Farms, a Navajo community, due to the high prevalence of tuberculosis and the population's lack of prior exposure to streptomycin, the main tuberculosis treatment at the time. The introduction of isoniazid marked the first time a cure for tuberculosis was considered feasible. Pyrazinamide is a drug used in the treatment of tuberculosis. It is primarily bacteriostatic but can exhibit bactericidal activity against actively replicating tuberculosis bacteria. Pyrazinamide is a prodrug that requires activation by the enzyme pyrazinamidase within Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This enzyme converts pyrazinamide into its active form, pyrazinoic acid. Under acidic conditions, pyrazinoic acid leaks out of the bacterium, becomes protonated, and reenters the bacterial cell, leading to its accumulation. This accumulation is more pronounced at acidic pH than at neutral pH. Pyrazinoic acid was initially thought to inhibit fatty acid synthase I (FAS I), an enzyme required for fatty acid synthesis in the bacterium, but this mechanism has been largely discounted. Instead, it is believed that the accumulation of pyrazinoic acid disrupts membrane potential and interferes with energy production, which is critical for the survival of M. tuberculosis in acidic environments. Pyrazinoic acid also binds to the ribosomal protein S1 (RpsA) and inhibits trans-translation, which may explain its ability to kill dormant mycobacteria. Resistance to pyrazinamide is primarily due to mutations in the pncA gene, which encodes pyrazinamidase. A smaller number of resistant strains have mutations in the rpsA gene. Rifampin inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA synthesis by binding to RNA polymerase at a site near its active center. This binding physically blocks the extension of RNA products beyond 2-3 nucleotides, a mechanism known as steric occlusion. Resistance to rifampin arises from mutations in the rpoB gene, which encodes the beta subunit of RNA polymerase. These mutations alter the rifampin-binding site, reducing the drug's affinity for the enzyme. Isoniazid is a prodrug that requires activation by a bacterial catalase-peroxidase enzyme called KatG in M. tuberculosis. KatG facilitates the coupling of isonicotinic acyl with NADH to form an isonicotinic acyl-NADH complex. This complex tightly binds to the enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase (InhA), blocking the natural enoyl-AcpM substrate and the action of fatty acid synthase. This inhibition prevents the synthesis of mycolic acid, a critical component of the mycobacterial cell wall. KatG activation of isoniazid also produces various radicals, including nitric oxide, which plays a role in the drug's action. Isoniazid is bactericidal against rapidly dividing mycobacteria but bacteriostatic against slow-growing ones. It also inhibits the P450 enzyme system. Pyrazinamide, as a prodrug, halts the growth of M. tuberculosis by being converted into pyrazinoic acid by the enzyme pyrazinamidase. Pyrazinoic acid accumulates within the bacterium under acidic conditions, disrupting membrane potential and energy production. While initially thought to inhibit fatty acid synthase I (FAS I), this mechanism has been questioned. Pyrazinoic acid binds to ribosomal protein S1 (RpsA), inhibiting trans-translation, which may explain its efficacy against dormant mycobacteria. Resistance to pyrazinamide is most commonly due to mutations in the pncA gene, with some resistant strains also harboring mutations in the rpsA gene.
